The phrase ma'dudah is understood as a sign of small value, since sums below an ounce were counted rather than weighed. As for the phrase that they were among those who were indifferent to him, most scholars apply it to the brothers, who did not know his standing with God, while al-Mawardi and al-Zamakhshari apply it to the caravan people who had picked him up and cared little for his price. The overall meaning is a concealed sale at a derisory price, a prelude to the establishment that God had decreed for Joseph.

This verse tells how the man who bought Joseph in Egypt told his wife to treat him well, since he might benefit them or they might adopt him. It then states that God established Joseph in the land and taught him the interpretation of events, meaning dreams, and that God prevails in His affair, though most people do not know. The commentators differ on the details of the sale. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the buyer was named Qitfir and that the seller in Egypt was Malik ibn Dhu'r, while al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi give similar accounts drawn partly from Israelite narratives. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi observe that the verb bought can mean exchanged or assumed, and that adoption was known among earlier peoples. All agree that the word mathwa refers to the place of lodging, and that honouring him means good food, fine clothing and a proper room. On the pronoun in 'His affair', al-Tabari and Ibn Juzayy refer it to Joseph, whereas Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and others refer it to God, who cannot be overcome. As for the 'most people' who do not know, some say they are disbelievers or polytheists, others that they are people in general. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur note that many of the detailed reports are not established by sound transmission, and that understanding the verse does not depend on them. The general meaning remains God's care for Joseph and the good outcome of his trial.

This verse states that when Joseph reached his full strength and the prime of his youth, God gave him wisdom and knowledge, and that this was a reward for his good conduct. The commentators differ on the length of the age called ashudd. Al-Tabari reports that Mujahid, Qatada and, by one chain, Ibn Abbas placed it at thirty-three years, al-Dahhak at twenty, al-Hasan at forty, Ikrima at twenty-five, al-Suddi at thirty, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr at eighteen, while Malik, Rabi'a, Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Sha'bi held that it means the age of puberty. Al-Tabari concludes that no evidence from the Quran, prophetic tradition or scholarly consensus settles the question, so the verse should be accepted as it stands. On wisdom and knowledge, Mujahid understood reason, understanding and insight before prophethood, while many took wisdom to be prophethood and knowledge to be religious understanding. Others read them as judging between people and interpreting dreams. Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir present the gift as a sign that Joseph was good in his actions. Razi argues that prophethood is not earned through deeds, so the verse cannot mean every righteous person would receive it. Commentators agree that the closing phrase applies to all who do good, and al-Tabari and others take it as a consolation and promise to the Prophet ﷺ.

This passage describes what happened in the house of the Minister when his wife sought to seduce Joseph, peace be upon him, and asked him to yield to her. She locked the doors and said to him, "Come!" Joseph replied by seeking refuge in God and explained his refusal: his master, who had treated him generously, must not be betrayed in his own household, and wrongdoers do not prosper. The commentators agree on this basic meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that "raawada" means to solicit gently and with cunning, and some report that there were seven doors. The phrase "hayta laka" has been read and explained in several ways. Most, including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, take it to mean "come" or "hurry to me". Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' considered it a Hawrani dialect word, while others saw Syriac or Coptic origins. Some read "hi'tu laka" as "I have prepared myself for you", a reading Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i rejected. On the word "rabbi", some understand God, others Joseph's master, as Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq do. The commentators report differing accounts of the "proof" (burhan) that Joseph saw, without deciding between them, and the question touches on the infallibility of prophets, discussed at length by al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya.

This verse recounts the episode of the minister's wife and Joseph, peace be upon him. The commentators explain that she desired to be with him, and that Joseph too was inclined toward her by human nature and the vigour of youth, had he not seen the proof (burhan) of his Lord, which restrained him. Most agree that hamm means desire or intention, and that the verse affirms Joseph's ultimate protection. On the nature of this proof the views differ. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada and al-Hasan report that he saw the image of his father Ya'qub biting his finger, while Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi says he read Quranic verses forbidding fornication written on the wall, and others mention the image of the king, prophethood, or the divine sign. Al-Tabari, after citing these, does not decide among them, saying it was a sign of God that restrained him and that it may have been Ya'qub's image, the king's, or the Quranic warning against adultery. Al-Shinqiti and Abu Hayyan hold that Joseph had no desire at all, the conditional clause negating it because he saw the proof, while al-Kashshaf and al-Qurtubi allow a natural inclination that was never acted upon. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn 'Ashur reject many reports they consider of Israelite origin. As for al-su' wa al-fahsha', some read it as betrayal of the master and adultery, others as its preliminaries. The reading al-mukhlisin with kasra means those who sincerely served God, and with fatha those whom God chose, both readings being considered compatible.

The verse describes the chase between Joseph and the wife of the nobleman as they rushed toward the door: Joseph hurried to escape and get out, while the woman caught up with him and tore his shirt from behind, and then they found her husband at the door, whereupon she immediately said that the punishment for anyone who intends harm to your household is prison or a painful torment. The commentators agree on the general meaning: the race was mutual, she trying to hold him back and he trying to flee, and the tear from behind shows that he was running away. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the witness who spoke was an infant in the cradle whom God gave speech, a view al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour by citing a hadith about those who spoke in infancy. Others, including al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid and al-Sudi, identify him as a wise man of her family or her cousin, a view mentioned by al-Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi, who discuss its implications. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain how the direction of the tear serves as evidence: a tear at the front suggests that he advanced, a tear at the back that he was turning away. Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi note that the word sayyid refers to the husband, and Ibn Ashur observes that the Copts used the term for a spouse. On how the testimony relates to the shirt, al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari weigh arguments without deciding between them, while modern commentators stress the clarity of the material evidence.

The Quran reports Joseph's words when the wife of the nobleman accused him: she was the one who sought to seduce me, and the commentators agree that he defended himself by speaking the truth. The judgment then came from a witness of her household, and the commentators agree that it rests on the sign of the shirt: if it is torn at the front, the woman speaks truly, because he came toward her and she pushed him away; if it is torn at the back, she lies, because she was pulling him while he was fleeing. The commentators differ on who the witness was. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Abu Hurayra and Hilal ibn Yasaf, whom al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy follow, held that it was an infant in the cradle whom God made speak, relying on the hadith of the four who spoke in the cradle. 'Ikrima, al-Hasan, Qatada and Mujahid, along with Ibn Ishaq, held that it was a wise, judicious man, sometimes said to be close to the king or to her family. Al-Suddi and Zayd ibn Aslam said he was her cousin, and others said her maternal cousin. Mujahid held that the witness was the torn shirt itself, a view Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari judged weak, since a shirt cannot be described as being of someone's household. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain that the word witness here means a statement that decides the matter. Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Shinqiti draw from the passage the principle of judging by circumstantial evidence, and al-Shinqiti notes that such evidence yields to stronger evidence, as in the blood-stained shirt of Jacob. Afterwards, the woman spoke of the punishment for anyone who intends harm to a household, Joseph cleared himself, and the lord told Joseph to keep the matter quiet and told his wife to ask forgiveness for her sin.

This passage shows how Yusuf cleared himself of the accusation. The commentators explain that a witness from the woman's family told the minister and those present: if the shirt is torn at the front, the woman speaks the truth and Yusuf is lying; if it is torn at the back, the woman is lying and Yusuf is truthful, since the one fleeing has his shirt torn from behind while the one pursuing has it torn from the front. When the minister saw the shirt torn from behind, he recognised Yusuf's innocence and his wife's falsehood. The commentators agree that a tear from behind proves Yusuf's sincerity, but they differ on who the witness was. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that he was an infant who spoke by God's will, relying on the hadith about four who spoke in the cradle. Others, such as Mujahid, Qatada, Ikrima and al-Hasan, say he was a wise man of her family. Ibn Abbas is reported to have said he was bearded and close to the king, and al-Sudi that he was her paternal cousin. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi favour the wise man, arguing that an infant's speech would itself be decisive proof. Mujahid held that the witness was the torn shirt itself, a view the commentators judged weak, since the verse describes the witness as one of her family. Ibn al-Qayyim drew from this verse the permissibility of judging by circumstantial evidence when no proof is available.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the moment the truth becomes clear to the wife's husband. Seeing Joseph's shirt torn from behind, he recognizes Joseph's innocence and his wife's falsehood, and he says that this accusation comes from the cunning of women, whose cunning is great. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, identify the speaker as the Aziz, the husband, while Ibn Abbas and others leave open that it may have been the witness. As for the witness who judged by the evidence of the shirt, opinions differ widely. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and Abu Hurayra say he was an infant whom God made speak, relying on a hadith that names Joseph's witness among those who spoke in the cradle. Al-Hasan, Ikrima, Mujahid and Qatada say he was a wise man of her household, al-Sudi and Zayd ibn Aslam say he was her cousin, and Mujahid in another report says the witness was the shirt itself. Al-Tabari favours the view that he was a child, while Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan find the shirt-as-witness view weak, since a shirt cannot be described as being of someone's family. Several commentators, including al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud, observe that women's cunning is more subtle and more penetrating than that of men, and they report a saying that one fears women more than Satan.

The ruler of Egypt tells Joseph to set this matter aside and keep it to himself, and tells his wife to ask forgiveness for her sin, since she was among those who had sinned deliberately. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the meaning as: do not mention what happened or speak of it to anyone, and you, ask your husband to pardon you and conceal your fault. The commentators agree that these words come after Joseph's innocence has been shown, and that their purpose is to close the matter and protect the family's reputation.

Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that some hold that it was the witness who settled the case who speaks these words, while others, such as al-Tabari, attribute them to the master of the house himself. As for the verb istaghfara, it may mean asking the husband for pardon or asking God for forgiveness, as Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi relate.

The masculine plural "al-khati'in" is, according to al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, a generalizing form in which the masculine takes precedence over the feminine. Al-Mawardi distinguishes between one who sins intentionally, described as khati'a, and one who errs without intent. Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi hold that the husband was patient and not very jealous, which explains why he limited himself to this rebuke. The commentators largely agree on the sense of the sentence itself; their disagreements concern who is speaking and how far the words bear on the judgment of the case.

God tells us that the story of the great official's wife and Joseph spread through the city, the capital of Egypt, until women of the notables spoke of it. They reproached her for seeking to make her young servant yield to her, saying that love for him had reached the innermost part of her heart and that they saw her in clear error. The commentators, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to al-Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur, agree that shaghaf means the covering or membrane of the heart, and that the sense is that this love had deeply seized her. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that there were four or five of these women, wives of senior court officials, while al-Mawardi records other views on their number and identity. They differ on what the shaghaf is: Ibn Abbas and al-Kalbi take it as a veil over the heart that love blocks out, al-Suddi as a thin skin on the heart, al-Hasan as the inner part of the heart, while al-Asma'i takes it to be an ailment below the ribs. The reading with 'ayn (sha'afaha), transmitted from Abu Raja' and al-Sha'bi, means for most that love drove her in every direction or burned her, as Ibn Ashur notes. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi report that these words were a scheme to bring Joseph before the women. The general meaning, for all of them, is a rebuke of the woman and a vindication of Joseph.

This verse tells how the wife of the great minister's word spread through the city, and how the women gossiped about her. When she heard their words, she invited them to her house, prepared a reclining place with cushions and food, and gave each of them a knife to cut fruit with. She then told Joseph to come out before them. When they saw him they were so overwhelmed that they cut their hands without feeling it, and they exclaimed: God forbid, this is no human, but a noble angel. The commentators broadly agree on this basic meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy stress the women's astonishment and confusion as the heart of the story. On the meaning of makr, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it as their slander, while Ibn Ishaq holds that they wanted to see Joseph; al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi also report that the woman had confided her secret to them. On the word mutaka', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as a seat or place to recline, Mujahid and Ibn Juzayy as food, al-Zamakhshari as a fruit such as the citron, and Ibn Kathir also cites Dahhak's view. On the phrase akbarna-hu, most render it as they exalted him, while one opinion, reported through Abd al-Samad, reads it as they menstruated, which al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi judge weak. On the cutting of hands, some speak of a mere scratch, others of a deep cut; al-Tabari holds that one should accept the plain wording. As for haasha lillah, readers differ on whether the alif is written, and the grammarians debate its nature.

The wife of the great official tells the women who cut their hands that this is the young man for whom they blamed her. She admits she solicited him, but he refused and kept himself chaste, and she threatens him with prison and humiliation if he does not obey her. The commentators explain that this confession comes because she now knows the women understand her. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi agree that the verb istasamma means that he held back and sought God's protection. For as-sagharin, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari take it to mean the humbled and the abased. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the final letter of wa-layakunan is a light nun, pronounced as an alif when pausing, in line with the written form of the Mushaf, while the emphatic reading is recited by some but considered contrary to the script. Al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari hesitate over the pronoun in ma amuruhu, which may refer to what she commands or to Joseph. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain that the demonstrative refers to the image of Joseph she describes. Opinions differ on fadhalikunna: al-Tabari takes it as Joseph present, while al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari take it as the image the women had formed of him. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi also relate what was said of Joseph's beauty, without choosing between these accounts.

Joseph, peace be upon him, prays to his Lord: prison is dearer to me than what they call me to; unless You turn their scheming away from me, I will incline toward them and be among the ignorant. The commentators agree that the one who solicits him is the minister's wife, and that the plural is explained either as a general reference to the women who pressed him or as a way of speaking indirectly. Al-Tabari, al-Wahidi and Ibn Kathir explain that «asbu» means to incline or to be drawn toward, and that «ignorant» means those who commit sin. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi note that the word «dearer» is not a true preference, since Joseph loved no sin, but a choice of the lesser of two evils. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi add that the verse shows his judgment of consequences. On recitation, Yaʿqub reads «as-sajn» with a fatha as a verbal noun, while most readers use a kasra for the noun of place; some readers read «asbu» from «sababa», meaning intense longing. Several scholars, including al-Qurtubi and al-Razi, cite the verse to say that a person refrains from sin only when God turns him away from it. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi mention the report that God told Joseph that had he asked for well-being it would have been granted. Al-Sa'di and al-Jaza'iri conclude that the verse teaches reliance on God, the wisdom of choosing the lesser harm, and the danger of ignorance of God.

The commentators explain that God answered the plea of Joseph, peace be upon him, when he sought refuge in Him from the women's scheming: He turned away from him what they wanted to draw him into, and kept him chaste. Al-Tabari, Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Kathir stress that he was saved from temptation and from falling into sin. Al-Tabari notes that his words, "And if You do not turn away from me their scheming," already contain an implicit request, which is why the answer is described without a plea being stated outright. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi observe that Joseph, by choosing prison over sin, turned to God's protection as the prophets and the righteous customarily do. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi hold that his steadfastness depended entirely on divine help, and al-Razi draws from this the view that a person turns away from wrongdoing only by God's grace. The closing words, "Indeed He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing," are linked by the commentators to the answer: God hears those who seek Him and knows their condition and what is good for them. Ibn Ashur sees in the particle "fa" a sign of the swift response. On the precise scope of the scheming, the commentators differ: some take it to refer to the minister's wife alone, with the plural used to honour her or to shift from direct to indirect speech, while others take it to refer to all the women, and the commentators leave that choice open.

The commentators explain that after the Aziz and his counsellors saw the signs of Yusuf's innocence, they resolved to imprison him for a period left unspecified. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Sam'ani and others identify these signs as the tearing of the shirt from behind, the scratches on the face, and the cut hands of the women; al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi add his beauty and chastity, and Ibn al-Jawzi also reports a witness's testimony.

Most exegetes link the imprisonment to the rumour spreading through the city, which the authorities wanted to end. Al-Suddi reports that the Aziz's wife asked her husband to imprison Yusuf as she had been confined, so that she could clear herself. Al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir also see the detention as a means of atonement for Yusuf's inclination, and cite Ibn Abbas on the three slips of Yusuf.

Opinions differ on the meaning of "hatta hin". Ikrima says seven years, al-Kalbi five, Sa'id ibn Jubayr six months, while Ata' understands it as until the gossip stopped. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi hold that the period is not fixed and that the figures are conjectures. Ibn 'Atiyya also reports that 'Umar objected to Ibn Mas'ud's reading "'atta hin", as a dialect of the Hudhayl, and ordered it recited in the Quraysh dialect.

Grammarians disagree on the subject of "bada": Sibawayh takes the clause "li-yasjununnahu" as the subject, al-Mubarrad posits an implied verbal noun, and al-Farra' treats it as an implied oath.

The verse tells that two young men entered the prison with Joseph. They were servants of the king, one his cupbearer and the other his baker, imprisoned on suspicion of plotting to poison him. Each recounted a dream: one saw himself pressing grapes into wine, the other saw bread on his head that birds were eating, and they asked Joseph to interpret them because they saw him as a man of good conduct. Most commentators take these as genuine dreams. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that Ibn Abbas and Mujahid held them to be true visions, while Ibn Mas'ud and al-Suddi held that the two invented them to test his knowledge. As for the word khamr, most explain it as grapes, citing Ibn Mas'ud's reading 'a'sir inaban' and the usage of the people of Oman reported by al-Dahhak, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as naming a thing by its eventual state. On the phrase 'of the good-doers,' opinions differ: al-Dahhak and Qatada understood Joseph's kindness to fellow prisoners, visiting the sick, comforting the grieved and easing the needy, whereas the majority took it to mean his knowledge of interpretation, and Ibn Ishaq took it as a promise of kindness in return. Al-Mawardi, al-Razi and al-Baghawi add that Joseph first told them what food would reach them, then called them to the worship of God alone, and only then interpreted the dreams, one announcing release and the other crucifixion. These commentators thus stress Joseph's wisdom in combining interpretation with his call to faith.

The commentators explain that when the two prisoners asked Joseph to interpret their dreams, he first promised that he would tell them the meaning of the food that would come to them before it arrived, and that this knowledge came from his Lord. On what the food refers to, al-Tabari, al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq take it to mean the food of their waking state or of the dream, while Ibn Juraij reports that the king used to send a known meal to those he wished to kill, which Joseph could recognise. Al-Hasan compares this knowledge to that of Jesus, who told people what they had eaten. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi see this announcement as a preface meant to lead the two men toward monotheism before answering their question. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi give several reasons for the delay, such as Joseph's wish not to reveal bad news to one of them, or to show that his knowledge exceeded that of ordinary interpreters, a view developed by al-Razi. As for the phrase about abandoning the religion of a people who do not believe in God, most read it as a voluntary turning away that does not imply he had ever taken part in it. The commentators agree that Joseph declares that he follows the religion of his fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, that monotheism is a favour from God to the prophets and to mankind, and that most people do not give thanks for it.

Yusuf, speaking to his two fellow prisoners, says that he has followed the religion of his forefathers Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub, and that God preserved them from associating anything with Him. The commentators treat this pure monotheism as a favour of God given to the prophets and to all people. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the favour toward Yusuf and his forefathers is that they were made prophets, and toward people that messengers were sent to them, while al-Mawardi offers another reading, that God kept Yusuf from fornication and from the sin of slander. They agree that tawhid is the thanks owed to God and that most people do not give thanks. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi hold that the word 'abandoning' does not mean that Yusuf once followed that path, but that he never entered it, although al-Razi also mentions the view that he concealed his faith out of caution before openly declaring it. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that Yusuf began with the call to faith before answering their question, so as to win their attention, and that he spoke as one inspired. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir relate the details of the prison and the dream interpretation, leaving judgement on these reports to the reader. Ibn 'Ashur stresses the continuity of prophethood in Yusuf's lineage. The general meaning is therefore shared: faith is a blessing from God that must be recognised with gratitude.

Yusuf, peace be upon him, addresses his two companions in the prison and poses a question that invites them to judge for themselves: is it better to worship many scattered lords, or Allah, the One, the Subduer? The commentators agree that the question aims to show the two men the falsehood of polytheism and to lead them to recognise that the One alone deserves worship. As for the phrase "companions of the prison", al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi take it to mean the inhabitants of the prison, while al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi take it to mean Yusuf's companions in prison, the prison being mentioned only as a place. Most identify the "scattered lords" as idols or multiple deities. Al-Qurtubi explains that the scattering refers to their differences in size, shape or number, and that a plurality of gods would lead to conflicting wills. Al-Razi presents it as a rational argument: idols are subdued rather than subduing, and a plurality of gods brings corruption. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi understand "the One" as having no rival and "the Subduer" as one whom none can overcome. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that Yusuf proceeds gently, starting from a simple point that the listener can accept before moving to weightier arguments. On the meaning of "names", Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi take these idols to be mere labels without divine reality, while others read it as referring to the idols themselves. All the commentators connect this passage with the call to monotheism that comes before the interpretation of the dreams.

Yusuf, in prison, tells his two companions that what they worship apart from God are only names that they and their fathers gave to idols, with no reality of divinity behind them, and that God has sent down no authority for them. Judgment belongs to God alone, who has commanded that He alone be worshipped; this is the upright religion. The commentators agree on the general meaning, a call to monotheism, and that most people do not grasp it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the names refer to idols called gods and lords for which there is no proof. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari read 'names' differently, as the essences themselves or as appellations empty of meaning, so that the worship is directed at labels without reality; Ibn 'Atiyya considers this the more likely reading, and Ibn al-Qayyim develops it. On the phrase 'the upright religion', al-Mawardi reports three views: the straight path according to al-Suddi, the clear reckoning according to Muqatil, and the true judgment according to Ibn 'Abbas. Several scholars, including al-Razi, see in the question about scattered lords a reference to the multiplicity of gods and their weakness before the one dominant God. Al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and al-Baydawi add that such worship is futile because these idols have no power. As to why most people remain ignorant, al-Razi links it to attributing events to the stars, while Abu al-Su'ud sees it as a refusal of plain reason.

Yusuf, peace be upon him, addresses his two companions in prison and interprets their dreams: one of them, the cupbearer, will leave prison and return to pouring wine for his lord the king, while the other, the baker, will be crucified and birds will eat from his head. The commentators explain that Yusuf left the condemned man unnamed so as not to grieve him. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, the phrase "the matter has been decided" means that what they asked about is now fixed and will come to pass. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Mas'ud report that the two men had invented their dreams to test Yusuf's knowledge and then denied them, while others such as al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that they had truly dreamed. On the meaning of "he thought" in "to the one he thought would be saved", al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy take it as certainty, while Qatada reads it as conjecture, since dream interpretation is a matter of conjecture. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur explain that a prophet may speak with certainty because he is inspired. As for the forgetting of the request to the king, opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas and most scholars attribute the forgetting to the cupbearer, while some attribute it to Yusuf himself, and Ibn Taymiyya, quoted by al-Baghawi, supports the first view.

This passage tells how Joseph, after interpreting the dreams of his two fellow prisoners, asked the one who would be freed to mention him to his lord, the king. Satan made him forget, and Joseph remained in prison for several years. Commentators differ on who is meant by the pronoun in « made him forget ». Most, including Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Taymiyya, take it to refer to the freed servant who forgot to mention Joseph to the king. Others, including Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan, take it to refer to Joseph, who forgot to rely on God alone and sought help from a created being. On the word « thanna » (thought), most say it means certainty, since the interpretation came by revelation, while Qatada takes it as ordinary supposition. On « bid' » (a few), the majority hold seven years, Mujahid and Qatada say three to nine, Ibn Abbas says fewer than ten, and al-Farra' says it is used only with tens. A hadith about God's mercy on Joseph is reported, but al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir judge it weak, and several commentators do not rely on it. Some see the forgetting as a punishment for seeking help from a human, while others hold that asking people for help in distress is permissible though unbecoming to prophets. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi record these views without a decisive ruling, and al-Alusi advises not to fix a precise duration.

This passage tells of the dream of the King of Egypt, which deeply disturbed him: he saw seven fat cows devoured by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain alongside seven dry ones. He then asked the notables of his court to interpret it for him. The commentators agree that this dream was a prelude to Joseph's release from prison, since it foretold years of plenty followed by years of famine. According to al-Tabari and al-Suddi, the king gathered magicians, priests, soothsayers and physiognomists, yet none could explain it. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that they replied it was a confused jumble of dreams, adghath ahlam, whose meaning escaped them. Al-Mawardi lists several meanings of the word adghath: mixtures, confusions, fantasies or lies, and cites a hadith distinguishing dreams from God from those inspired by Satan. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari hold that the notables did not wholly deny knowledge of interpretation, but judged this dream too disordered to be deciphered. Ibn Atiyya notes that the word for interpreting derives from crossing a river to its far bank, that is, reaching the end of a matter. The commentators do not oppose one another on the substance, and agree that the king genuinely sought an explanation.

In this verse, the chiefs of the king of Egypt, to whom he had described his dream of seven fat cows devoured by seven lean ones and of seven green ears of grain and others dried, reply that it is a jumble of confused dreams, meaning dreams without meaning, and admit that they cannot interpret such things. The commentators agree that adghath means a bundle of mixed herbs, a metaphor for tangled and false dreams that arise from the soul's own thoughts or from Satan's whispering. Ibn Abbas and Qatada take them to be lying or confused dreams, Mujahid to be frightful fantasies, and al-Hasan to be mixed colours. The plural 'dreams' for a single dream is explained by al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi as an exaggeration of its falsehood, or as a dream made of several parts. As for the phrase 'we are not learned in the interpretation of dreams', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud read it as a denial limited to false dreams, which have no interpretation, whereas Ibn al-Munir and al-Alusi take it as a general admission of the notables' limited knowledge. Ibn Sa'di notes that they spoke with certainty about what they did not know, and Ibn Ashur sees only a refusal to give an opinion.

This verse tells that the man who had been spared from the two prisoners remembered Joseph after a long time and offered to bring the king the interpretation of his dream. The commentators agree that the word 'umma' here means a long period of time, as Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ikrima explain, and as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari report. Some early readers read 'amah' meaning forgetfulness, among them Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Mujahid and al-Dahhak, and al-Tabari notes that the Arabs use the verb to mean forgetting; Ibn al-Jawzi observes that this reading implies that the cupbearer himself had forgotten. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the cupbearer may have held back from mentioning Joseph for fear of reminding the king of the offence that led to Joseph's imprisonment. As for his request to be sent, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir link it to the view of Ibn Abbas that the prison lay outside the city, while others say it was within it. Al-Razi explains that the cupbearer spoke tentatively because he feared that the other interpreters might fail and that he himself might not be believed. The commentators see in this passage the turning point that leads to Joseph's release, since the cupbearer's recollection opens the way to his deliverance.

After a long interval, the cupbearer who had been spared remembers Joseph and asks him to interpret the king's dream: seven fat cows eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain alongside seven dry ones. The commentators agree that the fat cows and green ears stand for seven years of plenty, and the lean cows and dry ears for seven years of drought. They also agree that Joseph advised leaving the grain in its ears to preserve it, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain. Most take the phrase 'after a long time' (ba'da umma) to mean a substantial period, and Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and al-Dahhak read it as forgetfulness, a reading al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi report without choosing between them. Al-Razi notes that some scholars said the cupbearer had concealed the matter out of fear of reminding the king of the offence that led to Joseph's imprisonment. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain Joseph's title 'the truthful' as a reflection of his proven honesty in interpreting dreams. The closing phrase 'so that they may know' is read by al-Mawardi and al-Zamakhshari either as knowing the interpretation or as knowing Joseph's rank and merit, which might win his release. Al-Tabari adds that the prison was outside the city, which explains the request to send for him. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that the commentators did not settle the exact length of Joseph's imprisonment.

Yusuf explains the king's dream: the fat cows and green ears stand for seven years of abundance, and the lean cows and dry ears for seven years of drought. He tells the people to sow during the good years as they usually do, to leave the harvest in its ears so that it is protected from rot and weevils, and to eat only a small amount. The commentators broadly agree on this plain meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the affirmative form as a command expressed as a statement, and regard the advice as a useful counsel rather than a binding obligation. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi hold that the statement form emphasises that the command must be carried out. The meaning of daʼb also divides them: most read it as steady habit, while al-Baghawi also reports the sense of diligence and effort. Several scholars, including al-Zamakhshari, treat the announcement of the eighth year as revealed knowledge, whereas Ibn Atiyya suggests it may follow from the very science of interpretation. The verb yaʻsiruna is taken by most as pressing grapes, olives and sesame, though al-Tabari and others mention milking or deliverance, and the readings vary between active and passive voice and between the second and third person.

Joseph tells the king that seven years of plentiful harvest will be followed by seven harsh years of drought, in which people will eat what they had stored, leaving only a small part of what they had kept safe. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, take the plain sense to be that the lean years will consume the reserves gathered in the years of plenty. Al-Tabari, following Qatada and Ibn Abbas, explains the word tuhsinun as storing and saving, while others take it to mean protecting seed for planting. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that attributing the eating to the years is a figure of speech, since it is the people who eat, as al-Razi observes, because a year does not eat. Abu Hayyan and al-Shawkani see the verse as the interpretation of the lean cows devouring the fat ones. Al-Razi and al-Mawardi also record the advice to leave the grain in its ears to keep it from spoiling and from weevils, which al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari also mention. The commentators agree that this warning belongs to the interpretation of the dream, whereas the promise of a rainy year with pressing that follows is, according to Ibn Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi, knowledge of the unseen given to Joseph. On the word yaʿsiruna, most take it as pressing grapes and olives, Ibn Abbas adds milking, and Abu Ubayda gives the sense of deliverance, which al-Tabari rejects.

Yusuf, peace be upon him, announces that after seven years of drought, in which the stored grain will be eaten, a year will come in which people will be relieved, meaning rained upon and freed from distress, and in which they will press what is pressed because of abundance. Most commentators understand the word ghayth as rain and see this year as a time of fertility and blessing. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that Ibn Abbas and Mujahid took the pressing to refer to grapes, olives and sesame, producing wine, oil and sesame oil. Ibn Kathir and others add that it may also mean milking the animals, a view also attributed to Ibn Abbas. Abu Ubayda and those who follow him, including al-Zajjaj, read the verb as meaning to be saved from hardship, citing a line of Abu Zubayd, but al-Tabari firmly rejects this reading because it contradicts the opinion of the Companions and Successors. On recitation, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the verb in the second person, while the rest read it in the third person. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Razi hold that the detail about this year comes from revelation, since the king's dream did not show it, while Ibn Ashur and others see it as a natural conclusion from the end of the famine. Qatada says God gave Yusuf knowledge of a year he had not been asked about.

The verse tells how the king ordered that Joseph be brought to him after the cupbearer had explained the interpretation of his dream. When the messenger came to bring Joseph out of prison, Joseph refused to leave until his innocence was made clear. He told the messenger to return to his master and ask about the women who had cut their hands, because his Lord knows their plotting. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that Joseph wanted the king to acknowledge that he had been jailed unjustly, so that no envious person could later attack his reputation. Most commentators present this patience as a virtue, and many cite the hadith in which the Prophet praises Joseph's forbearance while saying he himself would have answered at once. Al-Mawardi gives three reasons why Joseph did not name the minister's wife: to protect the wife of the king, because the women were witnesses against her, and to avoid suspicion. On the meaning of 'my Lord', opinion is divided: al-Tabari and most scholars take it to mean God, while some, including a second explanation of al-Tabari, take it to mean Joseph's master, the minister. Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari stress that Joseph acted with caution to guard against slander. Among the readings, some read the word 'al-nuswa' with a damma, which does not change the meaning. Ibn Kathir and others also relate that the minister's wife later confessed, which they see as confirming Joseph's innocence.

God tells us that the king gathered the women who had cut their hands and asked them what had happened when they tried to seduce Joseph. They cleared him, saying: "Far be God from it; we know no evil in him." Then the wife of the great minister declared: "Now the truth has come to light: it was I who sought to seduce him, and he is truly among the truthful." The commentators agree on the plain sense: the woman's confession and Joseph's vindication. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Abbas explain the phrase "now the truth has become manifest" as meaning that it became clear and evident. Al-Zamakhshari and others link the verb to the idea of a portion being separated from another, so that the truth was distinguished from falsehood. Al-Razi and al-Baghawi report that Joseph refused to leave prison until his innocence was established, which they count as a sign of his patience, and several cite a hadith praising him for it. Al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Taymiyya hold that the words "so that he may know I did not betray him in his absence" are spoken by the woman, while al-Razi, Ibn Atiyya and others attribute them to Joseph; Ibn Kathir prefers the first view because of the context. On why the women are addressed rather than the wife alone, the commentators give several reasons, including courtesy and discretion. Al-Zamakhshari uses the verse to argue for avoiding suspicion, while Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn Ashur see it as confirming Joseph's innocence through the admission of his adversary.

According to al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and several others, the verse means that this act of restraint or confession was done so that the master, or the king, would know that Joseph had not betrayed his master in his absence, and that God does not guide the schemes of traitors. Commentators differ on who is speaking. Most, including Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, hold that these are Joseph's words, explaining why he refused to leave prison until his innocence was established. Others, including al-Mawardi, Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Taymiyya as quoted by Ibn Kathir, attribute the words to the wife of the minister, who would be confessing that she had told the truth in Joseph's absence. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan find this second reading closer to the context, while al-Razi and Ibn Kathir note that the first is the more widely held. According to al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, this reading contains a veiled rebuke of the woman and the minister. Several scholars, including Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi, see the following sentence as an expression of humility and of refusing self-justification. The general sense is that God does not support the plotting of those who betray.

The commentators explain that the verse means a person cannot declare himself free of fault or certify his own purity, because the soul by nature commands evil and inclines to desire, and only one whom God shields is preserved from this. They differ on who speaks these words. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, attribute them to Joseph, who had just said, 'That he may know I did not betray him in his absence,' and then corrected himself out of humility and recognition of human weakness. Al-Tabari transmits accounts in which Gabriel or the king reminds him of his earlier inclination; al-Zamakhshari dismisses such reports as fabrications by those who slander the prophets, and Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi also find them weak. Others, among them Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Qayyim, al-Sha'rawi and Abu Hayyan, link the verse to the speech of the governor's wife, who admits to having pursued Joseph and excuses herself by saying the soul commands evil. Ibn Kathir calls this the most widely held and the best fit for the story, since Joseph was not present before the king at that moment. Ibn Ashur judges that both readings are possible and that the first suits a man filled with knowledge better. The exegetes agree on the meaning of the exception 'except those whom my Lord has mercy on', read as continuous or discontinuous depending on the view, and that 'ma' may mean 'those who'. The verse affirms that protection comes from God alone, and that God is forgiving and merciful toward whoever repents.

After Joseph's innocence was made clear, the king orders that he be brought so that he may be kept exclusively for his own service, apart from his other companions and counsellors. Having spoken with Joseph and recognised his wisdom and knowledge, the king tells him that he now holds a high rank in his presence and is trusted in everything. The commentators agree on this apparent meaning: the ruler draws Joseph close and entrusts him with authority. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya take 'makin' to mean high standing and position, and 'amin' to mean trustworthy and sincere. Ibn 'Abbas, as transmitted by al-Mawardi, understands it as real authority in the realm together with the trust that goes with it, while Abu Hayyan notes that being described as trustworthy is more honourable than merely being safe. Scholars differ on who the king is: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi identify him as al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, supreme ruler of Egypt, while others say it was al-Aziz; al-Razi and al-Tabari prefer the first view, since Joseph had earlier belonged to al-Aziz. The verse contains an ellipsis that the context clarifies, as Joseph is brought and then speaks with the king. Several reports cited by al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and others, such as Joseph washing and changing clothes when he left prison, or the conversation in seventy languages, are not considered authenticated even by the commentators who mention them. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan drew from this passage the permission for a virtuous man to seek office from an unjust ruler when he aims at justice, while others accepted this only with conditions.

Yusuf, peace be upon him, asks the king to place him in charge of the treasuries of the land, meaning the land of Egypt, presenting himself as a trustworthy guardian who knows how to manage them. The commentators explain that the treasuries are the stores of grain and wealth, and that the word "land" refers to Egypt, the definite article standing in for a possessive. On the meaning of "guardian, knowing", opinions differ: al-Tabari reports from Ibn Zayd, Qatada and Ibn Ishaq that it means he will guard what is entrusted to him and know its affairs, while as-Suddi takes it to mean skill in accounting and languages, and al-Kalbi takes it to mean sound planning for the lean years. Al-Tabari prefers the first sense, since the statement follows directly his request for the post and so should justify his competence.

The commentators agree that Yusuf sought this office out of concern for the public good, to establish justice and return rights to their owners, since no one else could do so. Ibn Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baghawi note that the king was then mostly not a Muslim, which led some scholars to derive from the verse a permission for a righteous man to serve an unjust ruler when he can do good, while others, such as al-Mawardi, set strict conditions on that permission. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur add that the story is also cited to justify seeking an office when no one else is fit for it.

Al-Razi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi explain that praising oneself is allowed when it serves a public interest and is free of pride, and Ibn Juzayy holds it permissible when a person's worth is unknown. Several commentators add that the narrations about the details of the appointment are not reliably authenticated.

The commentators explain that God established Joseph, peace be upon him, in the land of Egypt, so that he could settle wherever he wished after his imprisonment and hardship. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi largely agree that the mercy in the verse refers to worldly favours such as kingship and wealth, and that the good-doers are the patient and God-fearing believers, as Ibn Abbas and Wahb state. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the king appointed him in place of Qitfir, and Mujahid says the king embraced Islam through him. As for the phrase about settling wherever he wills, Sa'id ibn Jubayr understands it as choosing a dwelling in Egypt, while Ibn Zayd takes it as full delegation of authority; al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi say he came to control the whole land. Opinions differ on when the appointment took place: Ibn Abbas and Muqatil mention after a year and a half, whereas Wahb and Ibn al-Sa'ib say it was immediate. Accounts of the years of famine and the sale of the people's property appear in several works, but Ibn Kathir notes that they are Israelite narrations that can be neither confirmed nor denied. Ibn Kathir reads the verb with nun, while the majority read it with ya. On the reward of the Hereafter, al-Mawardi and al-Razi consider it better because it is lasting and pure, while Ibn Juzayy restricts the verse to this world.

This verse from Surah Yusuf states that the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and are mindful of God, after Yusuf had been granted authority in the land of Egypt. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that it refers to what God prepares for believers in the next life, which is greater and more lasting than what they receive in this world. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi take it as a call to make the Hereafter the true aim, since what Yusuf gained in this world is nothing beside it. The commentators agree that faith and God-consciousness are the condition for this reward, and that the verse follows the mention of good deeds and patience.

They differ on what the word "better" means. Al-Mawardi and al-Razi understand it as the lasting nature of the future reward against the ending of worldly rewards. Al-Razi adds that true good is pure, enduring benefit joined with honour, qualities found only in the Hereafter. A saying of Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, cited by al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan, holds that the believer is rewarded in both worlds, while the wrongdoer receives good in this world and has no share in the next. Al-Qurtubi applies the verse generally to every believing, God-conscious person.

About Yusuf himself, several commentators report accounts of his rule and his handling of the famine. Al-Baghawi, al-Tha'alibi and al-Qurtubi mention the king's conversion and the seizure of the Egyptians' property during the lean years. Ibn Kathir notes that some of these accounts belong to the Israliyyat, which can neither be confirmed nor denied. Al-Razi relates them without further judgment. On Yusuf's marriage to the minister's wife, al-Mawardi reports an opinion that he never married her.

The commentators explain that Joseph's brothers came to Egypt during the years of famine to buy grain, and entered upon Joseph while he held his office. He recognised them, while they did not recognise him. On how he recognised them, opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid say he knew them at the first look, while al-Hasan holds that he did not know them until they made themselves known to him. As for their failure to recognise him, most explain it by the long passage of time and his change of condition: they had left him a boy and found him a ruler, dressed in royal robes with a crown and a gold collar, according to what 'Ata' and al-Kalbi report. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya add the change of dress and status, the distance and their inability to imagine he had risen so high, while al-Razi suggests God may not have placed recognition in their hearts, as a confirmation of what Joseph had been told. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi mention that about forty years had passed since they cast him into the well.

The commentators agree that Joseph treated them generously, gave them full measure and demanded that they bring their brother Benjamin, failing which they would receive no more grain from him, and that they promised to win their father's consent. Ibn Ishaq and al-Suddi report that he ordered his servants to put their money back into their baggage. Al-Kalbi thinks he feared they would have nothing left to buy with, others that he disliked taking the price of grain from his father and brothers, and Ibn Kathir that he knew their piety would lead them to return it.

Al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan also note that the phrasing 'and they were unknowing of him' describes a lasting state of non-recognition, whereas his recognition of them came at once.

This verse tells how Joseph, after having the caravans of his brothers prepared and giving each of them a camel load, asked them to bring their brother from their father, meaning Benjamin, the full brother, while pretending not to know him. He encouraged them by saying that he gives full measure and is the best of hosts. The commentators explain that the custom was to give each man only one camel's load. They differ on the reason for the request. Ibn Ishaq and al-Suddi report that he questioned them about their family, al-Kalbi and Qatada identify the brother as Benjamin, and others suggest he wanted to see the son his father loved most. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that he meant to give an extra camel load for that brother, while al-Razi suggests he wanted to test their honesty. Mujahid explains that the phrase 'best of hosts' means the best of those who host. Joseph threatened that he would sell them no grain if they did not return with him. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Ashur mention that he demanded a surety, a detail which the sources record in various ways. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy explain that the brothers' reply, that they would seek their father's consent, is a firm promise to do so.

This verse reports that Joseph, after honouring his brothers, measuring out their grain and loading a camel for each of them, asks them to bring him their brother from their father, Benjamin. He promises to give full measure and generous hospitality, then warns them: if they do not bring him, there will be no measure of grain for them with him and they must not come near his land. The commentators explain that the measure refers to what would be sold to them in future, since their present load had already been given.

The commentators agree that Joseph's aim was to encourage his brothers to return and to deter them from coming without their brother. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn take "and do not come near me" as a prohibition, meaning do not enter my land. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan allow that it may be a negation linked to the conditional clause, meaning you will be deprived and will not approach. The brothers reply that they will try to persuade their father, which some commentators read as a firm pledge to do all they can.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy note that hunger was the reason for their journey. Al-Razi explains that the warning was severe because the brothers were in dire need of food. The commentators do not pass judgement on Joseph's conduct towards his father; they report the different reasons given for his actions without choosing between them.

God reports that Joseph's brothers, after Joseph had given them the provisions they had asked for and told them to bring their brother Benjamin from their father, answered that they would strive to persuade their father to send him with them, and that they would certainly do so. The commentators agree that the word rendered as 'we will seek to win over' means to press, to put great effort and to use stratagem in persuading the father. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain it as asking the father to let Benjamin go with them, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi take it as deceiving the father and wresting the boy from his hand. Al-Razi notes that the phrase can mean bringing him, or doing everything within their power. Ibn 'Ashur reads it as a promise to exert their utmost effort, with a hint that the task is hard. Ibn al-Jawzi gives three meanings of the verb: that they guarantee to bring him back, that it is emphasis, or that they will keep pressing their father. The exegetes also asked how Joseph could cause his father grief, and Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi give several answers. The one most favoured, by Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, is that God commanded it as a trial for Jacob to increase his reward. The commentators did not settle between these views and presented them as transmitted.

The verse reports that Yusuf told his attendants, the young servants who measured the grain, to put the price his brothers had paid back into their baggage, hoping that when they found it at home they would return to him. The commentators generally understand the fityan as servants or young attendants, and they differ on what the goods were. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada say it was silver coins, while a report from Ibn 'Abbas transmitted through al-Dahhak says it was sandals and leather, and others mention eight skins of ground dom-palm seed. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi prefer the view that it was silver. As for Yusuf's motive, al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi offer several explanations: fear that his father would have no money for another journey, a wish to ease the family's hardship during the famine, a sense that it was unworthy to take the price from his father and brothers in their need, or a desire to show his generosity so they would come back. Al-Razi adds the wish to remove any suspicion of theft and the expectation that their piety would make them return the money. Ibn Kathir considers these views close to one another and does not decide between them. On the recitation, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi explain that the plural forms fityatihi and fityanihi refer to the same servants, one suited to a small number and the other to a large one, and both are accepted readings.

The commentators explain that when Yusuf's brothers returned to their father Ya'qub, they told him that the governor of Egypt would withhold grain from them in future unless they brought their brother Benjamin. They therefore asked their father to send him with them, pledging to protect him. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi note that the words 'the measure has been withheld from us' may be understood as a warning about the future, or as an immediate refusal, since each man had received only one camel-load and Benjamin's share had not been given. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi say the grain would be refused until Benjamin came. On the reading 'nakhtal' with nun, followed by most readers, and 'yaktal' with ya', read by Hamza and al-Kisa'i, al-Tabari judges both to have the same meaning, while al-Qurtubi notes that the first includes all the brothers. Al-Mawardi, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir stress that Ya'qub, wary because of what had happened to Yusuf, did not trust them as he had before, yet he submitted to God: 'God is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful.' Ibn Kathir reads this as a hope that God would return his son to him. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan add that the variant readings of 'hafizan' and 'hifzan' concern grammar and leave the core meaning unchanged.

This verse records Ya'qub's reply after his sons asked him to send their brother Benjamin with them to obtain provisions. He tells them he cannot trust them with him as he once trusted them with Yusuf, and that God is the best guardian and the most merciful of the merciful. The commentators explain that Ya'qub is recalling that their earlier promises to protect Yusuf were broken, so he no longer relies on their word and entrusts the matter to God. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan, read these words as an expression of reliance on God and a plea for mercy, with hope that God will return his son to him. On the recitation, al-Tabari holds that the two readings, "hifzan" and "hafizan", are both well transmitted and close in meaning. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan explain that "hafizan" may be a specification or a circumstantial accusative, with al-Zamakhshari also permitting the latter. Al-Razi offers several reasons why Ya'qub eventually agreed to send Benjamin: his old age and the need for food, the absence of the envy that had existed between the brothers regarding Yusuf, and possibly a divine revelation. The verse thus shows both the father's anxiety and his surrender to God.

This passage describes the moment when Joseph's brothers opened their bags and found that the price of their goods had been returned to them. They said to their father: what more could we want? Here is our merchandise, returned to us; with it we will obtain provisions for our family, protect our brother, and gain the load of one more camel, a measure that is easy for the king to give. On the meaning of 'ma nabghi', the commentators differ. Qatada, al-Mawardi, Ibn Atiyya and al-Nasafi read it as a question: what more could we seek after such kindness? Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, and Abu al-Su'ud read it as a negation: we seek no other merchandise, or we do not exaggerate in what we say of his generosity. There is broad agreement that each man received the load of one camel, so the brothers asked for their brother to come in order to receive an extra load. Mujahid held that the word 'ba'ir' here means a donkey, a usage he attributed to some dialect, while most take it as a camel. As to 'that is an easy measure', al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir, and al-Baydawi take it as the brothers' words, meaning that the amount is small and the king will not be burdened by it; al-Razi and Abu Hayyan also take it as theirs, while some assign it to Jacob, meaning that one camel's load is not worth risking a son, a view Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan consider weak. A reading attributed to Aisha has 'ma tabghi' in the second person, addressed to Jacob.

This verse reports that Ya'qub agreed to send Benjamin with his sons only after they gave him a solemn pledge in God's name to bring him back, unless they should be encompassed, meaning overcome and unable to keep their word. The commentators differ on the meaning of being encompassed. Mujahid, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to mean being destroyed altogether, while Qatada, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir also report that it means being overpowered so that they cannot bring him back. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi treat the exception as limiting the only reason that could prevent the return. They generally agree that the covenant is an oath and a strengthened promise, and that naming God makes Him a witness to it. Al-Qurtubi draws from the verse a ruling on suretyship, which Malik and most jurists accept, though others limit or reject it. As for Ya'qub's words that God is a guardian over what they say, some read this as a witness, others as a guardian or guarantor of the oath, and al-Tabari adds that it is a reminder that God will reward faithfulness and requite betrayal. Ibn Ishaq explains that Ya'qub had no choice but to send his son because the grain was indispensable, and Ibn Sa'di notes that he relented after saying that God is the best guardian.

The commentators explain that when Ya'qub's sons prepared to leave for Egypt, he told them not to enter the city through a single gate but through several separate gates, adding that this precaution could not protect them from anything God had decreed, since judgment belongs to God alone, in Whom he trusts, and in Whom believers should place their trust. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy, understand that Ya'qub feared the evil eye for his sons because of their beauty and striking appearance, being eleven sons of one father, and they cite hadiths affirming that the evil eye is real. Al-Jubba'i denied it outright, which al-Razi and al-Nasafi considered unsupported, while Abu Hashim and al-Balkhi accepted it as a test for believers in the sense of divine wisdom. Al-Zamakhshari linked the fear to the special favour the brothers enjoyed at the king's court, and Ibn 'Atiyya mentions the fear of being suspected or entrapped, a view he considers weak. Regarding the statement that nothing can be averted from God, scholars agree that such precaution does not avert divine decree, and al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur stress that this does not mean abandoning worldly means. On Ya'qub's knowledge, Qatada understood it as acting upon what he knew, while others took it as keeping God's command in mind.

This verse recounts how the sons of Ya'qub entered Egypt by the separate gates their father had instructed them to use. The commentators agree that this precaution could not avert anything decreed by God, and that the need in Ya'qub's soul was his compassion and his fear that the evil eye might strike them, since they were handsome, well-built and sons of one man, as Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi add that the worry was also about their reputation with the king and about entering as one group, while al-Nahhas and some later scholars hold that he feared the ruler, seeing their number and strength, might seize them. Al-Zajjaj notes that caution does not repel destiny. On the phrase "he was truly possessed of knowledge by what We had taught him", al-Tabari explains it as knowledge taught by God, while Qatada, Sufyan and Ibn Kathir take it as acting on what he knew, and al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi also mention memorising it and certainty of God's promise. The closing words, "but most people do not know", are read by most as meaning they do not know what Ya'qub knew, whereas al-Razi and al-Nasafi take it as ignorance that caution does not avert destiny, and Ibn 'Ashur sees it as neglect of one of two duties, using means or trusting the decree. The commentators agree that the verse praises Ya'qub and honours knowledge, but they differ on the details of what he feared and on the meaning of the knowledge mentioned.

This verse describes the arrival of Yusuf's brothers before him. He takes his full brother Benjamin into his embrace, then privately tells him that he is his brother and bids him not to grieve over what the others did. The commentators agree on the core sense of the words: 'awa' means to take in or draw close, and 'tabta'is' means not to be dejected or sorrowful. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi, citing al-Suddi and Qatada, relate that Yusuf lodged the brothers in pairs, that Benjamin was left alone, and that Yusuf spent the night holding him and breathing in his scent. On the meaning of 'I am your brother', opinions differ. Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abbas, followed by al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, hold that he revealed to Benjamin that he was Yusuf, his real brother. Wahb ibn Munabbih, followed by al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, holds that he meant a brother in place of the lost one, without disclosing his identity. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi also report that he explained a plan to keep Benjamin with him, a point Ibn Kathir also records. As for 'what they used to do', some read it as the past wrongs done to Yusuf and Benjamin, others as what they would yet do, and others as their reproach over their grandfather's idolatry. Ibn Atiyya also mentions a reading that refers to Yusuf's servants and the cup, which Abu Hayyan considers unlikely. Ibn Ashur and Ibn Sa'di stress that the words were meant to calm Benjamin so that he would accept what followed without fear.

These verses describe how, after Joseph had fully equipped his brothers with provisions, he had the king's drinking-measure, called al-sigaya or al-sawwa', placed in the baggage of his brother Benjamin, and then a crier called out to the caravan that they were thieves. The commentators agree that sigaya and sawwa' refer to the same vessel, the one from which the king drank and which was also used as a measure for grain in a time of scarcity, and that al-ʿir means the caravan's people rather than only the camels. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi say the vessel was silver, while Ibn Zayd says it was gold, and Ibn ʿAbbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr mention other materials or a long measure like the Persian mikyal.

On whether the crier acted on Joseph's orders, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that he was unaware of the plan, whereas al-Mawardi, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan think it was done at Joseph's command, with the accusation perhaps referring to his earlier removal from his father. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi offer the reading that the phrase may be a question or a stratagem. The passage about the reward and the guarantee, a camel's load for whoever brings it back and I vouch for it, is taken by al-Mawardi and al-Nasafi as evidence that such a reward and surety were valid in the law of the time, though Ibn ʿAshur objects that Joseph had no revealed law to appeal to. Al-Tabari also stresses that the accusation fell on the whole party though only one of them was implicated.

This verse reports the reply of Joseph's brothers when the crier accuses the caravan of theft: they turn to the crier's men and ask what they have lost. The commentators explain that the lost item is the king's drinking-vessel, called ṣuwā' or siqāya, which was also used to measure grain. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi agree on this, and most say it was made of silver. Ibn 'Abbas and Ikrima describe it as silver set with jewels, Ibn Zayd says it was gold, and another report from Ibn 'Abbas mentions brass. Al-Zamakhshari adds that it was shaped like a long measure, the Persian mukkūk. As for the reward of a camel's load, most read it as a camel, while Mujahid notes that in one Arab dialect it means a donkey. Mujahid also takes the word za'īm to mean the crier himself. Jurists cite the verse as the basis for the ju'ala (reward) and kafala (surety), but Ibn 'Ashur doubts this, since Joseph had no revealed law of his own at that time. Al-Razi and others debate whether the crier acted on Joseph's orders or in good faith, and the scholars differ on this without a clear resolution.

The verse reports that the crier and his companions told Joseph's brothers that they had lost the king's cup, and that whoever brings it back will receive a camel's load of grain, and that the speaker vouches for it. The commentators agree that the sawa' was the vessel from which the king drank and with which grain was measured, and that the reward was offered to whoever returned it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya report that it was made of silver, and Ibn 'Abbas describes it as resembling the Persian mikkouk, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi cite other views, namely gold, copper, or jewel-studded. As for ba'ir, most say it means a male camel, though Mujahid holds that in one Arabic dialect it means a donkey. On who gave the guarantee, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir identify it as the crier himself, while Ibn 'Atiyya explains that since the food could only be found with the king, the crier took the pledge upon himself to make the offer credible. Jurists such as al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Qayyim drew from the verse the lawfulness of the reward contract (ju'ala) and of surety (kafala). Some asked how a guarantee could cover an unknown quantity, and answered that the camel's load was known to them. Ibn 'Ashur, however, considers that using this verse to establish these rules is questionable, since Joseph did not yet have a law of his own. The readings vary: sawa' is the common one, sa'a is attributed to Abu Hurayra, and sawgh to Yahya ibn Ya'mur.

This verse records the oath of Joseph's brothers when they were accused of stealing the king's goblet. They swear by God that the people know they did not come to the land of Egypt to cause corruption, and that they are not thieves. The commentators agree that the 'ta' in 'tallah' replaces the 'wa' and that it expresses wonder at the accusation. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi mention the signs of their integrity: they were known for uprightness, they muzzled their animals so they would not harm people's crops, and they returned the goods found in their saddlebags, which a thief would not have done. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi read 'you surely know' as an appeal to what people had witnessed of their conduct. On the meaning of 'to cause corruption', al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi take it as stealing, while al-Rabi' ibn Anas takes it as disobedience to God. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy report that the law of Ya'qub's family was to enslave the thief. Al-Qurtubi notes that some scholars regard that rule as superseded later by the punishment of amputation. Ibn 'Ashur doubts that this verse can serve as proof for the legal permissibility of the reward contract. The overall message is that the brothers defend themselves through their oath and through the evidence of their good character.

This verse records the question that Joseph's attendants put to his brothers once the king's cup had been found in their baggage: what is the penalty for the thief, if their denial proves false? The commentators explain that the pronoun refers to the thief or to the theft, by ellipsis. The brothers answer that the penalty is that the one in whose baggage the cup is found is taken and becomes a slave to the person robbed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that this was the rule of Ya'qub's family, whereas, according to al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Tha'alibi, Egyptian law required beating the thief and making him pay back double. These scholars note that this difference allowed Joseph to keep his brother with him. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari observe that the brothers thus accepted a heavier penalty than their own law required, since it applied to whoever was found with the object. On grammar, al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan propose several ways of parsing the sentence, without settling on one. Ibn 'Atiyya links the rule to collective responsibility. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya also stress that the verse is cited as a basis for the lawfulness of the reward and of surety. Ibn Juzayy notes that this rule of enslavement for theft was later abrogated by the penalty of amputation, and al-Qurtubi reports the same view. The commentators do not decide between these positions.

This verse records the answer given by Joseph's brothers when asked what the punishment should be for the one in whose baggage the cup is found. They say the penalty is that the one found with it be seized and enslaved, becoming the property of the one he stole from, and most commentators agree on this reading. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that this was the law in the family of Ya'qub, where a thief was handed over to his victim to serve for a year, whereas the law of the king of Egypt was to beat the thief and make him pay twice the value, as al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi note. The commentators agree that "his reward is that he in whose baggage it is found" is an affirmation and confirmation of the ruling, and that "thus do we requite the wrongdoers" shows that this was their custom toward thieves.

The grammar of "his reward" and "he who" divides the interpreters. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and al-Baydawi take "his reward" as the subject and "he who" as the predicate or second subject, so that the whole clause stands for a repeated pronoun, while al-Farra' and others propose different readings, and Abu Hayyan finds some of these analyses strained. For al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan the pronoun refers to the cup, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya takes it to refer to the thief.

Opinions also differ on the final phrase: al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy attribute it to Joseph's brothers, others to his attendants, and Ibn 'Ashur sees it as the continuation of their words. Ibn Kathir and al-Sha'rawi note that Joseph knew this law and allowed his brothers to pronounce the judgment that let him keep his brother with him.

This verse describes how Yusuf, by God's guidance, began searching his brothers' bags before that of his full brother Benjamin, to dispel any suspicion, and then drew out the king's bowl from Benjamin's bag. The commentators explain that this stratagem came from God: under the king's law of Egypt a thief was punished by a fine and beating, not enslaved, but the brothers themselves had pronounced the judgment of their own family's law, namely that the one in whose bag the bowl was found should be kept as a slave, which allowed Yusuf to hold his brother with them. The verse states that God raises whom He wills in rank through knowledge, and that above every possessor of knowledge there is one more knowing, until knowledge reaches God. The exegetes agree that Yusuf was the most learned of his brothers and that the word kayd here denotes a praiseworthy plan, not a blameworthy one. They differ on the meaning of the phrase din al-malik: Ibn 'Abbas took it as the king's authority, Qatada as his judgment and decree, and Mujahid as the law of enslaving thieves. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the custom of Jacob's family was to enslave the thief. Some reports mention an earlier accusation of theft against Yusuf which he kept to himself.
