Al-Zamakhshari compares the ruse to permissible legal stratagems, al-Razi sees it as a demonstration of the superiority of knowledge, and Ibn 'Ashur reads it as a divine inspiration given to Yusuf.

This verse records the words of Joseph's brothers when the cup was found in the baggage of their brother Benjamin: if he has stolen, a brother of his stole before him, meaning Joseph, a remark meant to clear themselves and cast blame on the sons of Rachel. The commentators agree that Joseph kept these words hidden within himself and showed no anger, and said inwardly that they were in a worse state than the ones they accused, and that God knows best what they claim. Most read the pronoun in "he kept it hidden" as referring to the remark or the accusation. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur take the phrase "you are worse in position" as the thing he concealed, while Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur also consider that Joseph may have answered them openly, and Abu Ali al-Farisi rejects the grammatical reading that makes the verse a case of pronoun explained by a following clause.

They differ on what theft was meant. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada say he broke an idol of his maternal grandfather, al-Hasan says they were simply lying about him, and Mujahid relates that his aunt kept him by hiding Isaac's belt on him. Other reports mention a piece of meat, an egg or a hen given to a beggar. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi transmit these accounts without choosing one, and Ibn Juzayy lists them as possibilities. Ibn Kathir notes that such details come from Israelite reports, and no sound statement from the Prophet identifies the theft.

Joseph's brothers address the governor of Egypt after it has been settled that Benjamin will be detained. They remind him that their father is a very old man who loves this son and finds comfort in him after losing another, and they ask that one of them be taken in Benjamin's place, praising the governor as a man of goodness. Al-Tabari and Ibn Ishaq explain that 'we see you among the good-doers' means he has done good to them in his dealings, such as giving full measure, treating them well and returning their goods, while al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi understand it as meaning that if he does this, he will be among the good-doers. Al-Razi adds the possibility that it refers to his kindness to the whole people through the freeing of slaves. Commentators differ on 'an old man, very aged': al-Mawardi, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir take it to mean someone of high standing or advanced years, whereas al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Ashur stress his extreme old age. As for 'take one of us in his place', most explain it as holding someone as a pledge or in servitude; Ibn Atiyya, followed by Abu Hayyan, suggests a figurative sense or a surety, since prophets would not want to enslave a free man. All report Joseph's reply, 'God forbid that we take anyone but him with whom we found our property', and that taking an innocent in place of the guilty would be wrongdoing. Ibn Ashur notes that Joseph, for reasons of caution, did not reveal his identity at that time.

This verse records Joseph's reply when his brothers asked that one of them be held in place of Benjamin: "God forbid that we take anyone except him with whom we found our property; otherwise we would indeed be wrongdoers." The plain meaning, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain, is a refusal to seize an innocent man for a guilty one. They all note that Joseph did not say "the thief" in order to avoid lying, and that "ma'adha Allah" is a verbal noun. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi explain that the wrongdoing lies in placing the penalty where it does not belong. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud add an inner meaning: God had commanded Joseph to keep Benjamin for reasons He knew, so taking another would go against the revelation. On the brothers' request, opinions differ. Ibn 'Atiyya holds it to be hyperbole, since enslaving a free man is not lawful, while al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan read it as a real request for a pledge or security, and Ibn Juzayy compares it to a surety. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi also discuss suretyship in legal penalties. On the word "ihsan", al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take it as gratitude for past kindness towards the brothers, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan read it more broadly. The commentators agree on the moral lesson: the innocent must not be punished for the guilty.

When the brothers of Joseph despaired of getting Benjamin released, they withdrew to confer in private. Their eldest, whom the commentators identify differently, reminded them of the solemn pledge they had given their father before God and of their earlier failure regarding Joseph. He declared that he would not leave the land of Egypt until their father permitted it or God judged for him, for God is the best of judges. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take him to be Ruben, the oldest in age, while Mujahid names Shimon for his standing and judgment, and Ibn Abbas and al-Kalbi name Yahuda for his wisdom. Al-Tabari concludes that age is the most likely meaning of "eldest", since the Arabs use the term unqualified to mean either rank or age. Grammarians differ on the particle "ma" in "what you neglected": some treat it as superfluous, others as a verbal noun or a relative pronoun, each with a different sentence structure. On "or God judges for me", Abu Salih understood it as taking up arms, whereas most commentators read it as departure from Egypt or the release of their brother by some means. The exegetes agree that the verse expresses a firm resolve to remain in Egypt until one of these outcomes occurs.

The eldest of Joseph's brothers tells the others to go back to their father Jacob and tell him that his son Benjamin has been accused of theft after the king's goblet was found in his baggage, and that they testify only to what they witnessed: they saw the goblet taken out of his sack. They add that they could not know the unseen, meaning they could not have foreseen this when they gave their pledge. The plain sense, held by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, is that they report an observed fact without claiming knowledge of what was hidden from them. Mujahid and Qatada explain that not guarding the unseen means they never suspected the theft. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take it that they were certain of the theft, since the cup was drawn from the bag, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi read it as a testimony based on a strong apparent suspicion that stood in for knowledge. On the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Razin and al-Kisa'i, surriqa in the passive, the meaning is that he was charged with theft without the speakers claiming certainty, a view al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan report. Ibn Zayd says the point concerns the law of Jacob's household, under which a thief is enslaved. Some commentators gloss ghayb as night in the dialect of Himyar, a meaning al-Tabari says he could not find in lexicons and Ibn 'Atiyya considers unusual.

In this verse the brothers of Joseph tell their father to question the town where they were, which the commentators identify as Egypt, and the caravan they travelled with, whose members were men from Canaan, neighbours of Jacob. Al-Tabari, Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Kathir take this as an invitation to ask the people of the town and of the caravan, who could confirm what happened; Ibn Kathir adds that the caravan could vouch for their honesty and trustworthiness. Al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi mention that the town may have been a village near Egypt where the announcement had been made. Most commentators, including Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Ashur and al-Alusi, see an ellipsis in which a word such as people is omitted, so the phrase is a figure of speech. Al-Razi gives the same view, and cites al-Anbari, who suggests that the walls and the caravan could be asked directly, since inanimate things may address a prophet. Al-Qurtubi quotes Sibawayh's objection that such an omission is not acceptable, and Ibn Atiyya and al-Alusi regard the literal reading as far-fetched. As for the closing words, we are truthful, al-Baydawi sees an emphasis close to an oath, while al-Razi explains that the brothers do not prove their honesty by their word alone but offer evidence first. Ibn Sa'di reads the verse as an invitation to verify what they say.

This verse records Ya'qub's reply to his sons after they returned from Egypt without their brother Benjamin. He tells them that their own souls had made an affair seem fair to them, he calls his patience a beautiful patience free of complaint, and he hopes that God will bring back to him all three sons: Yusuf, Benjamin and the eldest who stayed in Egypt. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Zamakhshari, agree that Ya'qub suspected them of a scheme and did not accept their account. They differ on what the embellished affair was: Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi see it as an evil assumption about them, while al-Razi understands it as the decision to take Benjamin to Egypt, which brought harm. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that beautiful patience means not complaining to people, and al-Qurtubi notes that a believer must meet calamity with patience and submission. Regarding his hope, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir link it to the return of Yusuf, whereas al-Razi and al-Qurtubi stress his trust in God and mention a possible sense that Yusuf was alive. The scholars conclude that God knows Ya'qub's condition and that of his sons, and that He is wise in disposing of their affairs.

This passage describes Ya'qub (Jacob) turning away from his sons after hearing the news about their brother, and lamenting in grief, saying, "Alas, my sorrow for Yusuf!" Commentators explain that the word asaf means intense grief mixed with regret. They differ on the meaning of the cry: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean "O my grief" or "O my distress", while al-Mawardi records two readings, either a complaint addressed to God alone or a supplication asking God to relieve this sorrow. On his eyes turning white, all agree that it resulted from weeping caused by grief. Yet al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn Juzayy say he lost his sight, Muqatil says he could not see for six years, whereas al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and others mention only a weakening of his sight. The word kazim is understood in several ways: one who suppresses his grief without revealing it, according to Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya; one who is overwhelmed, according to al-Tabari and Ibn Juzayy; or one who is consumed with sorrow, according to Qatada and Mujahid. Several scholars, including al-Qurtubi and al-Qasimi, distinguish between grief, which is not blameworthy, and wailing and lamentation, which are. The commentators agree that Ya'qub showed perfect patience and never doubted God.

This verse records that Ya'qub's sons, seeing the depth of his grief for Yusuf, said to him under oath: "By Allah, you will not cease remembering Yusuf until you are close to death or die." The commentators agree that the verb "tafta'" means "to keep on doing," and that the negation is implied, since an oath without the lam and nun signals negation, a point illustrated by the verses cited by al-Tabari, al-Nahhas and Ibn al-Jawzi. The word "harad" is explained in several ways: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak take it as one who is wasted by illness or worn by age, Mujahid as close to death, al-Hasan and Qatada as old age, Ibn Ishaq as loss of reason, al-Farra' as a body and mind in decay, and Abu 'Ubayda as one melted by grief or love. These definitions are close, all describing a decline of body and mind caused by pain, love or sickness. On "or be among the dead," all the commentators agree that it refers to death.

According to al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and others, the sons meant to show concern and to soften his grief. Al-Tabari and Ibn Juzayy add that the oath rested on strong conjecture. Ya'qub replies that he complains only to Allah: al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that "bath" is extreme sorrow, which Ibn 'Abbas glosses as worry and al-Hasan as need.

Many commentators relate reports about Ya'qub's patience and his grief, including those cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Suyuti, which they judge weak or problematic. The exegetes do not settle between these reports and simply record them.

This verse reports that Ya'qub, after turning away from his sons who wondered at his grief, told them that he complains of his sorrow and distress only to God, not to them or anyone else, and that he knows from God what they do not, namely that relief and mercy are near. The commentators agree that the word bath means a grief so intense that it cannot be concealed: al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as a sorrow that cannot be hidden, while Ibn 'Abbas understands it as worry and al-Hasan as a need. As for the phrase 'I know from God what you do not', Ibn 'Abbas, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir link it to the truth of Yusuf's dream, al-Suddi and others to Ya'qub's sense that Yusuf is alive, and some report a story about the Angel of Death, whose chain Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi judge weak. On the blindness, Mujahid and others speak of total loss of sight, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi prefer a weakening of vision caused by constant weeping. Al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi explain harad as one wasted away or close to death, and kazim as one who restrains his grief. On whether such sorrow is blameworthy, al-Razi and al-Alusi note that weeping is natural and only complaining to creatures is condemned, while Ibn al-Qayyim sees in it an example of trust in God.

Ya'qub tells his sons to go and seek news of Yusuf and his brother, and not to despair of God's mercy, since only the disbelieving people despair of it. The commentators agree that tahassus means to seek something by the senses and to inquire carefully. The word rawh here means relief, deliverance and mercy after hardship, as Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd explain. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi mention the reading min ruhi Allah with a damma and take it to mean the mercy by which God gives life to His servants, while Ibn 'Atiyya suggests that one does not despair of a living person in whom God's breath remains.

Several scholars report that Ya'qub still hoped Yusuf was alive. Al-Suddi relates that he asked the angel of death, who said he had not taken Yusuf's soul, and al-Qurtubi builds on this view. Ibn Kathir cites a report of a true dream, and al-Razi lists several signs that gave Ya'qub this hope.

Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur note that most jurists consider despair of God's mercy a major sin, though the verse describes it as a trait of disbelievers rather than saying that whoever commits it becomes a disbeliever. Al-Alusi remarks that the verse does not clearly prove this in itself. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir also note that tahassus is used for seeking good and tajassus for seeking harm.

The commentators explain that Joseph's brothers, arriving in Egypt, addressed him as al-'Aziz, described the famine that had struck them and their families, and said they had brought a meagre, inferior merchandise that would only be accepted at a discount. They asked him to give them full measure and to be generous, concluding that God rewards those who give charity. For them, the verse is a plea built on a description of their hardship.

The commentators agree that the goods described as muzjāt are a small or poor quantity that people reject, and that the root izjā' means to push or drive away. Al-Tabari and others cite verses by al-Nabigha, A'sha Bani Tha'laba and Hatim to support this sense. On what the goods actually were, opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas says they were counterfeit dirhams accepted only at a loss, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith says wool and clarified butter, Abu Salih says pistachios and green seeds, al-Dahhak says ground doum-palm flour, and others mention hides, sandals or ropes.

As for the request « and be charitable to us », there are three main readings. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, al-Hasan and most exegetes take it as a request to overlook the poor quality of the goods and to be paid as if they were good. Ibn Jurayj and al-Dahhak take it as a request for the return of their brother. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna holds that charity was permitted to earlier prophets before Muhammad ﷺ, while Mujahid says it was forbidden only to the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Tabari keeps the common meaning of charity as a gift, though he considers the reading about the brother's return to be a valid view.

The verse describes Yusuf, moved by his brothers' appeal and their complaint of hardship and meagre goods, letting his tears flow and revealing himself with a gentle rebuke: do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother, when you were ignorant? Al-Tabari explains that the ignorance refers to not knowing where Yusuf's affair and their own would lead. Ibn Kathir and most commentators take the question as an assertion meant to magnify the gravity of their deed and to rebuke them, not as a request for information. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi specify that their treatment of the brother meant separating him from his full brother and subjecting him to many kinds of harm. Ibn 'Atiyya suggests the ignorance may be ignorance of sin or the inexperience of youth. Al-Mawardi gives three meanings: the ignorance of childhood, the ignorance of sins, and ignorance of the consequences of their acts. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said they were young, while Muqatil described them as sinners. Several scholars, including al-Baydawi and al-Alusi, held that the speech was counsel and encouragement to repent rather than reproach, softening their shame. They differ on what moved Yusuf to reveal himself: Ibn Ishaq attributes it to his compassion, while others point to his father's letter or another event.

This verse records the moment Joseph, after confronting his brothers about what they had done to him and his brother, reveals himself. They ask in astonishment whether he is truly Joseph. He confirms that he is Joseph, names his brother, and attributes to God the favour that reunited them after separation. He then explains that whoever fears God and endures patiently, God does not waste the reward of the good-doers. On the plain meaning, the commentators largely agree. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the brothers recognised him once the veil was lifted or the crown removed, revealing a mark on his forehead, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi treat the question as a request for confirmation and explain recognition through his appearance, his smile, or his features. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir prefer the majority reading as an interrogative, and Ibn Kathir stresses that it conveys astonishment. On the meaning of piety and patience, Mujahid takes it as avoiding sin and enduring prison, Ibn Abbas and al-Nakha'i take it as chastity and patience in celibacy, and others take it more broadly as fear of God and patience in calamities. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the term good-doers covers those who combine piety and patience. Ibn al-Jawzi observes that the phrase I am Joseph points to the wrong done to him. These differences concern details rather than the overall sense of the verse.

This verse records the brothers of Joseph acknowledging his superiority over them after he made himself known. They say: by God, God has preferred you over us, distinguishing you with knowledge, forbearance, intellect, beauty and sovereignty, and we were sinners in what we did to you. Al-Tabari and al-Suddi take this to mean that they had acted deliberately and sinned. Al-Mawardi and Ibn Atiyya distinguish between the khati', who sins knowingly and is culpable, and the mukhti', who intends the right but fails to reach it. Ibn Abbas holds that whoever sins deliberately strays from the truth until he falls into doubt and disobedience. Ibn al-Jawzi and others suggest that they were apologising mainly for concealing the matter from their father after they grew up. Al-Razi reports that Abu Ali al-Jubba'i held they did not apologise for throwing Joseph into the well, which occurred before puberty, but for their later silence.

The commentators agree that this confession is followed by Joseph's pardon: there is no reproach against you today. They differ on the meaning of tathrib: Sufyan ibn Uyayna takes it as change of feeling, Ibn Ishaq as rebuke, Mujahid as refusal, al-Zamakhshari as damage to honour, and al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya as censure or punishment. They also differ on whether 'today' attaches to the reproach or to the forgiveness. Abu Hayyan and Ibn Atiyya prefer pausing after 'today', since tying forgiveness to that day would amount to judging God's mercy.

Yusuf tells his brothers, who have just admitted their wrongdoing, that there is no reproach against them today, and he prays that God forgive them, for He is the most merciful of the merciful. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain "tathrib" as blame and rebuke, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi, followed by al-Baydawi, derive it from "thirb", the fat covering the entrails, and read it as a figure for a harsh reproach that strips away honour and dignity. The commentators agree that the verse is a generous pardon for the past, granted because the brothers sincerely confessed. They differ over the word "today". Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan link it to the blame: on this day, the very occasion when reproach would be expected, there is none, so all the more on other days. Others, including al-Zamakhshari as an alternative, link it to "God will forgive you", reading the phrase as good news of forgiveness granted that day. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan prefer pausing at "today", since joining it to the forgiveness clause would pass judgement on God's pardon. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir treat the second clause as a supplication, while Ibn Kathir notes the brothers' earlier repentance. Al-Razi observes that the closing phrase may refer to God's favour in raising Yusuf to power or to His pardon of the brothers. Al-Qasimi draws from the verse a lesson in forgiving those who wrong us.

Joseph tells his brothers to take his shirt to their father and lay it on his face so that his sight will return, and then to bring the whole family to him. The commentators report that Jacob had gone blind from weeping over Joseph, and that this act was the means of restoring his sight by knowledge from God. On the shirt itself, as-Suddi, Mujahid and Muqatil say it was the shirt Joseph was wearing, while ad-Dahhak, Ibn 'Abbas and others say it was Abraham's garment brought from Paradise, passed down to Isaac and Jacob, and hung on Joseph's neck; Ibn 'Atiyya judged it more likely to be an ordinary shirt of Joseph. The phrase 'yaʼti basiran' is read by al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda as 'he will return seeing', and by az-Zajjaj and others as 'he will become seeing' or 'he will come to me seeing'. Al-Kalbi puts the household at around seventy people, while Masruq gives ninety-three. The next verse reports that when the caravan left Egypt Jacob smelled Joseph's scent; the commentators differ on the distance, with Ibn 'Abbas saying eight days' journey, al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj eighty farsakhs, and others ten days. The meaning of 'lawla an tufannidun' is also debated: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid explain it as 'you would call me foolish', al-Hasan as 'you would call me senile', Ibn Zayd as 'you would say I have lost my mind', and others as 'you would call me a liar'. at-Tabari concludes these meanings are close, since the root signifies corruption.

This verse describes the moment the caravan leaves Egypt for Canaan, when Ya'qub tells those around him that he smells Yusuf's scent, while fearing they will mock him as senile. The commentators agree that this perception was an extraordinary event, but they differ on how far the scent travelled: Ibn 'Abbas puts it at eight days' journey, al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj at eighty farsakhs, Mujahid at three days, and others give other figures. Some explain that the fragrance of the Paradise-garment reached Ya'qub, while others say the wind itself asked its Lord to carry the scent to the father. The meaning of the word tufannidun is also debated: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it as 'you will call me foolish', al-Hasan as 'you will think me senile', Ibn Jubayr as 'you will call me a liar', Ibn Qutayba as 'you will criticise me', and Ibn Zayd as 'you will say your mind has gone'. The words of those present, calling Ya'qub lost in his old love for Yusuf, are read by Ibn 'Abbas as an error, by Qatada as excessive attachment, and by Ibn Jubayr as madness. The messenger is identified by most as Yahuda, and the commentators report that Ya'qub postponed his prayer for his sons' forgiveness until the pre-dawn hour or the night of Friday.

This verse records the reply of those around Ya'qub after he said he could smell Yusuf's scent. They swore by God that he was still in his old error. Most commentators agree that 'dalal' here does not mean disbelief but a mistake or an excessive preoccupation. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd and al-Tabari take it to mean error, while Qatada and Sufyan take it to mean his old love for Yusuf, which he never forgot. Muqatil reads it as hardship and suffering, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr as madness. Ibn 'Atiyya considers such words too harsh to be said to a father, and reports that Qatada called them a rough remark that should not have been spoken. Al-Samani and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that the speakers believed Yusuf was dead and saw Ya'qub's constant mention of him as confusion. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the speakers were grandsons or other relatives present, since his sons were away in Egypt. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read the expression as a departure from the right course caused by an intense love. The commentators share the broad picture of a father overwhelmed by longing, and relatives who judged him to be misguided.

This verse describes the moment the bearer of good news arrives and throws the shirt over Jacob's face, and his sight returns after he had lost it. Jacob then tells his sons and those around him that he knows from Allah what they do not know, namely that Yusuf is alive and that Allah will reunite them. The commentators broadly agree on this plain meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the bearer was Yahuda, son of Jacob, who had earlier carried the blood-stained shirt and now wished to gladden his father as he had grieved him, while al-Dahhak and Mujahid, in one transmission, call him simply a messenger. Ibn Abbas names Malik ibn Dhu'r, and al-Mawardi also gives Shim'un as a possibility. On the restored sight, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that Jacob had gone blind and regained his sight, whereas al-Razi says his sight had only weakened from weeping and grew strong again through joy. Al-Razi also reads Jacob's words as referring to his knowledge of Yusuf's life from the dream. Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan suggest that the reference may instead be to his remark about smelling Yusuf's scent or to his command not to despair of Allah's mercy. Concerning the particle 'an' in the phrase 'lamma an', al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya regard it as superfluous, while Ibn Qayyim explains its function as emphasis. The commentaries leave these points open for the reader to weigh.

Yusuf's brothers ask their father to seek God's forgiveness for their sins, admitting that they were wrong in what they did to Yusuf. The commentators agree that such an admission is the first step to repentance, and that the one who confesses his wrong deserves to be pardoned, as al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud note. Ya'qub, for his part, postpones his promise to intercede, and al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that most exegetes, such as Ibn Mas'ud, Ibrahim al-Taymi, 'Amr ibn Qays and Ibn Jurayj, hold that he delayed it until the last part of the night, the time when prayers are answered.

Opinions differ about the exact time. Ibn 'Abbas, in a report that al-Tabari traces to the Prophet though Ibn Kathir considers it weak, names Friday night, Sa'id ibn Jubayr mentions the bright nights of the month, and al-Sha'bi says Ya'qub wanted first to ask Yusuf whether he had forgiven them. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya add that he may have wished to test the sincerity of their repentance.

Sayyid Qutb and al-Sha'rawi observe that this delay let hearts calm and grievances settle before the pardon was granted.

Ya'qub, peace be upon him, answers his sons, who had asked him to seek forgiveness for their sins, by saying that he will ask his Lord to forgive them, adding that He is the Forgiving, the Merciful. The commentators agree that he did not refuse to pray for them, but postponed the prayer to a time when it is more likely to be answered. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Sam'ani report, through Ibn Mas'ud, Ibrahim al-Taymi and Ibn Jurayj, that he delayed it until al-Sahar, the hour before dawn when people call upon God; this view is also attributed to Ibn 'Umar, Qatada, al-Suddi and Muqatil. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi transmit another opinion, reported from Ibn 'Abbas, that the time was the night of Friday; Ibn Kathir considers the attribution to the Prophet questionable. According to al-Sha'bi, he first wished to ask Yusuf whether he had forgiven them. Al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya also mention seeking the blessing of his prayer, and the idea that the elderly need more time than the young to obtain what they ask. Ibn 'Atiyya stresses that forgiveness depends on sincere repentance, a point that al-Zamakhshari, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Nasafi connect with testing the sincerity of their repentance.

This passage describes the meeting of Jacob and his family with Yusuf upon their arrival in Egypt. Yusuf drew his parents close to him and told them to enter Egypt, God willing, in safety, meaning free from famine and every harm. He then raised his parents onto the throne, and his brothers fell prostrate before him as an honour. Yusuf recognised in this the fulfilment of the dream of his youth, in which eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowed to him, and he thanked God for freeing him from prison and bringing his family from the desert after Satan had stirred discord between him and his brothers. God is gentle in what He wills, and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise. The commentators agree that the prostration was a greeting of honour and not an act of worship. As for the identity of 'his two parents', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya find it more apparent that they were his father and mother, while as-Suddi, Wahb and Ibn Juzayy hold that it was his father and maternal aunt, his mother having died. On the phrase 'if God wills', as-Suddi links it to a moment before they entered the city, Ibn Jurayj reads it as a displaced phrase, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi connect it to the safety rather than the entry. Opinions also differ widely on the length of time between the dream and its fulfilment, ranging from forty to eighty years and other figures according to the reports.

This passage describes the moment Joseph reunites with his parents and brothers on their arrival in Egypt. He draws his parents close to him, seats them on the throne, and they and his brothers fall down in prostration before him. Joseph tells his father that this prostration is the fulfilment of the dream he had long ago, in which eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowed to him, and that his Lord has made it true. He then recounts God's favours: He brought him out of prison and brought his family from the desert after Satan had stirred discord between him and his brothers. He ends by affirming that his Lord is subtle in what He wills, and that He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise. The commentators agree that this prostration was an act of honour and greeting, not worship. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that the two parents were the father and the stepmother, since the mother had died, while Ibn Ishaq holds that they were the father and the true mother. Opinions differ on the time between the dream and its fulfilment: Salman al-Farisi and Abdullah ibn Shaddad say forty years, al-Hasan eighty, and Ibn Ishaq eighteen. On the phrase 'if God wills', al-Tabari links it to entering Egypt in safety, while Ibn Jarir reports it is tied to Jacob's plea for forgiveness. Ibn Abbas understood 'badw' as the desert, while others take it as a place named Bada. Joseph does not mention the well out of delicacy towards his brothers, and the commentators judge that his release from prison was the greater favour, since it led him to power.

After Yusuf has been reunited with his parents and brothers and given power and knowledge, he turns to his Lord with praise: My Lord, You have given me some of the kingdom and taught me the interpretation of narrations; Originator of the heavens and the earth, You are my guardian in this world and the next; let me die in submission and join the righteous. The commentators agree on the general sense: the kingdom is only part of royal power, and the interpretation of narrations is mostly understood as the interpretation of dreams. Fatir means the Creator who brings things into being, and wali means the protector who manages one's affairs. They differ on the request for death. Qatada and a report from Ibn Abbas understand it as a longing to meet God, so that Yusuf would be the first prophet to ask for death, and al-Razi notes that a wise person may wish for death when he sees the emptiness of worldly pleasures. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, by contrast, take it as a request to be taken in Islam without wishing for death itself, and some cite the prophetic prohibition of wishing for death because of harm. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain submission as remaining in Islam until the end. As for the righteous, some say they are the people of Paradise, others his forefathers Ibrahim, Ishaq and Yaqub, and others all the righteous including the prophets. The reports on how long he lived and where he was buried are numerous, and the commentators relate them without deciding between them.

The commentators explain that this verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ: the story of Joseph and his brothers is one of the reports of the unseen, which he did not witness and knew only through revelation from God. He was not present with the sons of Jacob when they resolved together to cast Joseph into the bottom of the well, scheming against him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari see here first a way of strengthening the Prophet's heart and proving the truth of his mission, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan also detect an ironic note aimed at the Quraysh and at those who called him a liar, since he had never studied such accounts.

Most agree on the meaning of the key terms: ijma' al-amr is the firm resolution reached, and makr is a plan that harms another. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi allow that the scheming may also target Jacob, when the brothers brought him the shirt stained with false blood; Ibn Abbas, by contrast, understands it as the sons of Jacob alone. Ibn al-Anbari, quoted by Abu Hayyan and al-Shawkani, reports that the Quraysh and the Jews asked the Prophet about this story, which he related hoping for their conversion, and that the verse came to console him when they refused.

Commentators generally link this verse to what follows, where it is said that most people will not believe however much one desires it. Ibn Ashur notes that the present tense of the verb for scheming evokes the scene vividly.

The commentators explain that this verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ after the story of Joseph and his brothers: most people will not believe, however much you strive to guide them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari take it to refer to the people of Mecca or to unbelievers in general, who persisted in refusal and obstinacy, while al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya see it as a rebuke to the Quraysh and as a proof established against them. Ibn al-Anbari and those who follow him report a occasion of revelation: the Quraysh and the Jews asked the Prophet about the story of Joseph, he explained it in agreement with the Torah, yet they did not embrace Islam; he was saddened, and God consoled him with this verse. On the meaning of 'hirs' (eagerness), al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya understand it as intense desire, while al-Zajjaj explains that guidance rests with God. A majority, including Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, hold that the following verse about associating partners with God concerns Arab pagans who acknowledged the Creator yet worshipped others alongside Him; some apply it to the People of the Book, and Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari report that it also concerns the polytheists' talbiya. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir conclude that complete faith is rare, and that the call is made without reward.

The commentators explain that God addresses His Prophet ﷺ, telling him that he does not ask his disbelieving people for any wage or reward for conveying the message and calling to God, so that no one may suspect him of seeking worldly gain. The Qur'an is only a reminder and an admonition to all the worlds, through which they may be warned and guided, which makes it a pure benefit for people. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi understand the wage as material gift, with the true reward resting with God alone. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi hold instead that the reminder benefits those who hear it, since it contains their salvation. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi stress that the admonition is addressed to everyone in general, which fits with not charging for it. All agree that dhikr means admonition and reminder. Ibn 'Ashur restricts the address to the people of Mecca and those he was sent to, while most others see all of humankind. Some readers recite the verb with an initial nun. The pronoun in 'alayhi' refers to the Qur'an, to the report, or to the conveying of the message, depending on the view. Some exegetes draw from it a lesson for preachers: to convey the truth without payment.

The commentators explain that God points out that many signs of His oneness and power are spread across the heavens and the earth, such as the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the seas and the plants, as well as the traces of the destroyed nations. People pass by these signs and see them, yet they turn away from them without reflecting or taking lessons. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir explain this turning away as people's heedlessness towards reflecting on what creation reveals about its Creator. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the turning away concerns many signs in the universe, not just one, and that 'passing by' here means seeing and observing. Ibn 'Atiyya links the passage to consoling the Prophet ﷺ over the unbelief of most of his people.

The commentators agree that this verse is connected to the one before it, and that its original audience is the polytheists. They differ over the meaning of the following verse, 'And most of them do not believe in God without associating others with Him.' Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, 'Ikrima and Ibn Zayd took it to mean the Arab polytheists who acknowledge that God created and sustains them yet worship other gods alongside Him, and al-Tabari supports this with the verse 'If you asked them who created them, they would say God'. Others, including al-Hasan and, in another report, Ibn 'Abbas, applied it to the People of the Book who associate 'Uzayr or the Messiah with God, or to hypocrites who feign faith. Al-Hasan also saw in it those who act for show. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy note that there is a hidden form of association, such as showing off, swearing by other than God, or amulets. Al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir also report that the verse refers to the prayer made in distress, when people sincerely call on God in hardship and then associate others with Him once it is lifted. Ibn Kathir adds that most commentators consider these readings all included in the general meaning of the verse.

This verse states that most people, even while acknowledging God as their creator, provider and the creator of the heavens and earth, associate others with Him in worship, by worshipping idols and images, or by ascribing partners and children to Him, and God is exalted above that. It comes in a context where people pass by the signs of creation without reflecting on them.

The commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrima and Qatada, largely agree that the faith of these people consists of acknowledging God as creator and provider while still worshipping others. Ibn Kathir reports that the idolaters used to say in their talbiya: "Here I am, You have no partner, except a partner who belongs to You, whom You own and who owns nothing." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Sha'bi apply the verse to the Meccans, al-Hasan to hypocrites who show faith while concealing disbelief, and others to People of the Book who worshipped 'Uzayr and the Messiah. Al-Hasan also holds that showing off in deeds is a hidden form of association.

Some scholars, such as al-Sam'ani and Ibn al-Jawzi, explain that "faith" here means linguistic faith or outward profession rather than true belief. 'Ata' takes the verse as referring to supplication: disbelievers forget their Lord in ease, then sincerely call upon Him in hardship.

This verse asks, in the form of a rebuke, whether those who feel secure can be sure that a punishment from God will not overtake them and cover them, or that the Hour will not come upon them suddenly while they are unaware. Most commentators understand the "ghashiya" as a punishment that envelops and covers. Mujahid and al-Tabari say it overwhelms them, Qatada says it is a calamity that falls upon them, and al-Dahhak says it means thunderbolts and calamities. Ibn Abbas, as transmitted by al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, describes it as a punishment that covers everything. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report from Ibn Abbas that "the Hour" is the Day of Resurrection, which will seize people while they are in their markets. Al-Tabari reads the verse as addressing polytheists who acknowledge God as creator yet associate others with Him. Al-Mawardi, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi record several views on who is meant by the wider context: the Quraysh, the People of the Book, the hypocrites, or those with hidden polytheism, as Ibn Kathir notes. On the general sense, the commentators agree that the verse warns against heedlessness of the consequence, whether in this world or on the Last Day. Ibn Ashur sees the question as a reproach. The commentators do not settle the question of identity, but they share the warning's purpose.

This verse has the Prophet ﷺ declare that his path is to call to God alone, with insight and clear proof, and that those who follow him call to the same. On the meaning of "path," Ibn Abbas, al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak take it as the call itself, Ibn Zayd as the sunna and method, and Muqatil and most commentators as the religion; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir treat these meanings as close to one another. On "insight," most explain it as certainty and clear evidence, while Qatada reads it as guidance, and al-Mawardi reports that some understood it to mean only delivering the message without the power to guide hearts. The commentators differ on where to pause. Al-Farra', al-Kalbi, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir take "those who follow me" as joined to the subject of "I call," so that the followers too call to God, a view Ibn al-Qayyim finds the most eloquent. Ibn al-Anbari and others stop after "to God" and read "with insight, I and those who follow me" as a new clause. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi treat "I" as emphasis, while Abu Hayyan, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi set out several grammatical options. All agree that "Glory be to God" declares God free of any partner or offspring, and that "I am not among the polytheists" disavows shirk. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi connect the preceding verses to Quraysh, the People of the Book, or polytheist talbiyah chants, though this background is not needed to understand this verse.

This verse states that God sent before you only men, drawn from the people of the towns, to whom He revealed His message: not angels, not women, and not desert nomads, according to most commentators. It urges people to travel the earth and see the fate of the peoples who rejected their messengers, and it declares that the abode of the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful of God. The commentators agree that the word qura means towns and cities rather than the desert, and al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi cite Qatada and Ibn Zayd, who held that townspeople are more knowledgeable and gentler. Al-Hasan, al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir add that no prophet was a jinn or a woman. On female prophethood, Ibn Kathir reports the majority view that there were none, only truthful women such as Mary, while others point to Sarah, Moses' mother and Mary. As for the phrase the abode of the Hereafter, the Kufans treat it as an adjective-noun construction, while the Basrans supply an omitted noun such as the future life; al-Razi, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi discuss this grammar. In the next verse, the readings differ: those who read the verb without the doubling attribute the doubt to the messengers or their peoples, while Aisha, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi reject that prophets could have doubted their Lord, and Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report these debates. Most read the verb as fa-nunajjī, while Abu Ubayd prefers the single-nun spelling of the Uthmanic codex.

This verse describes a settled pattern in God's dealings with His messengers: victory may be delayed until the messengers despair of their people's faith and their followers think they have been lied to about the promise, and then God's help arrives, saving whom He wills, while His punishment is not turned back from the guilty people. The commentators differ mainly over the last word. The reading "kudhibu" with a light stress is ascribed to Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid and the Kufan readers, and the reading "kudhdhibu" with a heavy stress to others, including 'A'isha, who defended it. On the light reading, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, following the majority, take the doubt to belong to the peoples who thought the messengers had lied about the punishment. Reports from Ibn Abbas say the doubt belonged to the messengers themselves, a momentary human weakness, which al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir reject and al-Razi finds too far-fetched. On the heavy reading, 'A'isha holds that the messengers feared their followers had denied them after long trials, and Qatada, al-Hasan and al-Zamakhshari read "zann" as certainty. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir favour this reading. Most commentators identify those whom God saves as the messengers and their believers, and see the verse as consolation for the Prophet ﷺ and a warning to his opponents. Several note that the text speaks of men from the towns rather than women, angels or nomads, because townspeople were judged wiser and more patient, following Qatada and Ibn Zayd.

The commentators explain that this verse concludes the story of Yusuf and his brothers and that it contains a lesson for people of sound intellect, in what befell Yusuf through trials and then empowerment. They also state that the Quran is not a fabricated tale but confirms the revealed books that came before it, explains everything people need, and is guidance and mercy for believers. Most agree that the pronoun in 'their stories' refers to Yusuf and his brothers, though Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj hold it refers to Yusuf and his brothers in particular, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan prefer the stories of all the messengers. Ibn 'Atiyya notes the pronoun may cover all messengers mentioned in the surah. Regarding 'not a fabricated tale', Qatada takes it to mean the Quran, while Ibn Ishaq takes it to mean the stories already narrated. As for 'confirming what was before it', most identify the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms, while some identify the Quran itself. Some scholars read 'confirmation' in the nominative, making it a predicate. The phrase 'every thing' is understood by some as the lawful and unlawful, commands and prohibitions, and by others as all that religion requires. Al-Sha'rawi and others stress that the lesson moves the reader from the visible to the hidden. Guidance and mercy are specified for believers because they alone benefit from them. These views converge on the lesson, the Quran's truthfulness and its completeness.
